data.title: Dutch Jobless Rate Remains Stable At 4.0%
data.description:
BRUSSELS (dpa-AFX) - The Netherlands' unemployment rate held steady for the third straight month in October, data from the Central Bureau of Statistics showed on Thursday.

The seasonally adjusted ILO jobless rate stood at 4.0 percent in September, the same as in the previous three months. In the corresponding month last year, the rate was also 4.0 percent.

There were 414,000 unemployed people in October compared to 408,000 in the prior month. A year ago, it was also 408,000.

Data showed that the net labor force participation rate stood at 75.9 percent in October, down from 76.1 percent in September.

data.title: Fed Credibility Seen Intact — Market Talk
data.description:
0716 GMT - The Federal Reserve's credibility looks intact because inflation expectations have barely moved even as policy-rate expectations rise, BNY's John Velis says in a note. "Markets still expect the Fed to address inflation, but the cost of maintaining credibility may be excessive restraint," the Americas macro strategist says. Velis adds that the rates markets' focus has become more specific, with an interest-rate hike in December being the main policy scenario markets are focused on, while the path beyond December is unclear. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0652 GMT - Rates are not high enough to justify a bullish duration call, Barclays rates strategists say in a note, keeping a neutral view. "Inflation has been firm, Federal Reserve communication has become more hawkish, growth remains resilient and risks assets are unlikely to collapse," they say. Barclays stays overweight equities over bonds. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0644 GMT - Relief in French government bond yield spreads is still possible with the timely passage of a 2027 budget, even if by decree, ING's Benjamin Schroeder says in a note. However, any relief is unlikely to be a lasting one ahead of the French presidential elections in April, the senior rates strategist says. The 10-year French OAT-German Bund yield spread closed at 147 basis points on Wednesday, according to LSEG. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0641 GMT - Bitcoin and ether rebound a little after bottoming out following the release of the Fed's October FOMC minutes, which came out hawkish. Bitcoin is 1.9% higher at $63,442 after reaching as low as $62,086 in the previous session, while ether rises 2.2% to $1,801.50. Investors expect the Fed to raise interest rates in December, making nonyielding assets, including cryptocurrencies, more expensive to hold. Traders are pricing in a 90% chance of a quarter-point rate hike in December, with a 10% chance of a half-point rise, according to CME FedWatch. (joseph.wilkins@wsj.com)

0621 GMT - Bitcoin's drawdown cycle looks shallow so far, says digital-asset banking group Sygnum. The correction is contained against falls of more than 70% in previous cycles, Sygnum says in a report. By contrast, the drawdown from the latest high in October 2025 to the current bottom is roughly 54%. If Bitcoin doesn't fall below the June/July low this cycle, it would be the shallowest of any bear market to date. While it's too early to say whether the cycle has run its course, the asset class still seems to be entering 2027 with lower structural volatility, stronger fundamentals and clearer, if still incomplete, regulation, says CIO Fabian Dori. Bitcoin gains 1.8% but stays around three-month lows at $63,428. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0603 GMT - Morgan Stanley is constructive, but not complacent, about risks assets in 2027, amid more clarity on two of the big unknowns that have weighed on the markets this year, its analysts say in a note. "The U.S. midterms are behind us, with investors now being able to focus on a narrower set of outcomes, even if the results don't necessarily mean reduced policy volatility," they say. After the Federal Reserve's interest-rate hike in September, "markets now also have a better read of Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's reaction function even if there will likely be less forward guidance in the future." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0601 GMT - Quality is the reason why Morgan Stanley remains neutral on U.S. Treasurys, despite the fact that it is maximum overweight in global equities, its analysts say in a note. "In fact, we keep some exposure to duration because we are max overweight in stocks," they say.As much as there has been a lot of concern that stock-bond return correlations are now stuck in a positive regime and Treasurys have lost their shine as a buffer in the portfolio, "we think this concern is overdone." Bonds have acted as a ballast against the most recent tech sell-off, served their purpose during the cross-asset deleveraging event in February this year, they say, adding that U.S. Treasurys remain a good portfolio diversifier. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0600 GMT - Crypto prices are now more exposed to liquidity shocks, even as the underlying asset became less volatile, according to Sygnum Bank analysts. The maturing of the crypto industry has changed how shocks are propagated, they say. "Shifts in liquidity and risk appetite now travel through [exchange-traded funds] redemptions, the reversal of digital asset treasury companies' capital raising, the unwinding of leveraged basis trades and margin calls on crypto-collateralised credit," the analysts write. Liquidity remains one of the dominant forces to determine bitcoin's price as a shortage of it can compound forced selling, according to Sygnum. (joseph.wilkins@wsj.com)

0600 GMT - Cryptocurrencies are increasingly trading off the full dollar liquidity picture, Sygnum Bank analysts write. Central bank policy rates, long-end yields and the term premium are all influencing cryptocurrency prices. U.S. Treasury cash management, bank balance-sheet capacity and offshore dollar funding conditions are also cited as potential drivers. With financial conditions tight and geopolitical risk elevated, asset performance is likely to remain tethered to the dollar-liquidity cycle, the analysts write. (joseph.wilkins@wsj.com)

0600 GMT — The era in which a rising tide lifted all digital assets is drawing to a close, according to Sygnum Bank. The next phase is likely to have winners and losers, as outperformance has become idiosyncratic across the different coins, Sygnum analysts say. While bitcoin sat roughly a third below its all-time high through late September 2026, major other coins rallied, indicating that bitcoin's trajectory no longer leads the wider cryptocurrency market. "With bitcoin dominance anchored near 60%, and ETF flows concentrating capital at the top of the market capitalization curve, there is no longer a window when all altcoins rally together," the analysts write. (joseph.wilkins@wsj.com)

0530 GMT - Malaysia's stronger-than-expected 3Q GDP growth is unlikely to materially raise the probability of a Bank Negara Malaysia rate increase in January 2027, CIMB economists Chew Khai Yen and Michelle Chia say in a note. Private consumption growth has moderated, while uneven services activity and easing services inflation point to limited demand-driven price pressures, they say. BNM is likely to remain focused on the inflation outlook, particularly amid upside risks from higher production costs, weather disruptions as well as coming income and wage measures, they reckon. CIMB expects 4Q GDP growth to moderate to 5.1% from 5.5% in 3Q. It raises Malaysia's 2026 growth forecast to 5.5% from 5.0%, but maintains its view that the policy rate will stay at 2.75% in January. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0435 GMT - Malaysia's 2027 GDP growth could moderate but remain resilient, supported by household spending, higher government development expenditure and sustained demand for electronics and electrical products, CGS International Mas Aida Che Mansor says in a note. Government assistance programs, minimum wage increases and tourism spending should support consumption, while infrastructure projects and electricity grid investments are expected to support construction activity, she says. Strong global semiconductor demand should also sustain exports and manufacturing, though growth may moderate, she reckons. While a more protectionist U.S. trade stance could weigh on global trade and manufacturing, the impact of recent U.S. chip licensing rules on Malaysia's growth is expected to be minimal, she adds. CGSI maintains its GDP growth forecasts at 5.5% for 2026 and 4.7% for 2027. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

data.title: Japan Tobacco to Book $8.6 Billion Loss on Russia Business
data.description:
By Kosaku Narioka

Japan Tobacco expects to book an $8.6 billion loss after losing control of its Russian business.

The Japanese tobacco maker said Thursday that it can no longer make business decisions concerning its operations in Russia in the same manner as before.

Earlier this month, Japan Tobacco said all seven of its Russian entities had been placed under temporary administration by a Russian company on the orders of President Vladimir Putin.

The move marked an escalation in Russian measures against Japanese businesses following Tokyo's support for Ukraine and its participation in Western sanctions against Moscow over its 2022 invasion.

Japan Tobacco on Thursday projected a net loss of Y724.00 billion, equivalent to $4.54 billion, for 2026, primarily due to a special loss of Y1.377 trillion related to the loss of control of its Russian business.

The company's Russian operations had about Y1.5 trillion in assets, including goodwill and roughly Y360 billion in cash and deposits, as well as about Y200 billion in liabilities at the end of September, the company said.

Japan Tobacco had expected Russia to account for about 10% of its revenue and 25% of adjusted operating profit in 2026.

The Japanese company was previously a state-owned monopoly, but the government held just under 38% of its shares at the end of 2025.

Japan Tobacco, whose brands include Winston and Camel, is one of Russia's largest tobacco companies, with a market share of nearly 40%.

Write to Kosaku Narioka at kosaku.narioka@wsj.com
